bib.title: Operationalizing Machine Learning: An Interview Study

question: What does operationalizing ML (MLOps) involve in practice across organizations and applications, and what are the unaddressed challenges for tool builders?
contributions: Identifies four routine tasks (data collection, experimentation, evaluation and deployment, monitoring and response) and three variables for success: Velocity, Validation, Versioning
Summarizes common practices for experimentation, evaluation and sustaining production performance
Describes pain points, anti-patterns and a four-layer MLOps tool stack with implications for tool design

method.summary: Semi-structured ethnographic interviews with 18 ML engineers, transcribed automatically by Zoom, redacted, then coded with open and axial coding (grounded theory) in MaxQDA by two study personnel until convergence. Findings are organised around the Three Vs.
method.task: qualitative interview study of production ML workflows

datasets.name: Interview transcripts
datasets.size: 18 interviews, 45 to 75 minutes each; 1766 coded segments, 600 unique codes
datasets.source: MLEs recruited via professional networks and MLOps Discord, Slack and Twitter; unpaid; audio and video not recorded; transcripts redacted of PII

inference.samples: 18 participants; recruitment in rounds of 3 to 5 candidates over an academic year (2021-2022) until saturation

parameters.coding: two personnel independently coded; passes top-down or bottom-up; repeated until convergence
parameters.code_correlation: two codes correlated if within twenty sentences

eval.protocol: Grounded theory open and axial coding in MaxQDA; saturation of findings used as stopping rule; no inter-coder agreement statistic reported; counts of participants given per finding as (P#) lists

availability.data: Not released; transcripts held in a secured drive (privacy). Interview questions in Appendix A.

limits: Sample of 18 MLEs recruited from professional networks and MLOps communities; authors flag the 22% female skew as possible sampling bias
Self-reported practices; no quantitative measurement of outcomes or inter-coder agreement
Interviews date from 2021-2022, before LLM-based products were common (only chatbot, NLP examples)
Participants could not share exact numbers (e.g. deployment durations) for privacy
Authors leave unexplored which classroom skills would help

terms.definition: the 'set of practices that aim to deploy and maintain ML models in production reliably and efficiently'
Velocity (prototype and iterate fast), Validation (test and prune early), Versioning (keep multiple model and dataset versions for debugging and fallback)
predictions generated live but not surfaced to users, before a deployment to a small fraction of live users
assuming during training that there is access to data that does not exist at serving time
hard: obvious bad predictions e.g. swapped columns; soft: e.g. a few null features; drift: live data from a seemingly different distribution, slowly over time
Service Level Objectives, commitments to minimum standards of performance for pipelines
